title: Nostalgia hinders Takaichi's vision for Japan
gist: Bill Emmott argues Japan's PM Sanae Takaichi has replaced Abenomics with a METI-planned Y370 trillion (US$2.25tn) 15-year industrial programme across 17 strategic sectors, which is inherently inflationary and will force the Bank of Japan to raise rates and push up the cost of capital for both government and corporates. He flags incoherence — a consumption-tax cut to 1% on food and a push to make the GPIF absorb JGBs — while defence policy shows straighter thinking, including an open debate on scrapping the third non-nuclear principle and building a Japanese external intelligence service from scratch.

insights.claim: Japan's 'Takanomics' abandons the Abenomics three-arrow framework of fiscal expansion, monetary expansion and structural reform in favour of an old-fashioned industrial-plus-fiscal policy mix executed on a very large scale.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Investors modelling Japan on the Abenomics playbook — reflation via BoJ balance sheet and a weak yen — are using the wrong template for the next decade.
insights.quote: her ‘Takanomics’ turns out to consist of an old-fashioned mix of industrial and fiscal policy, albeit on a grand scale
insights.locator: The biggest nostalgia-fest lies in economic policy

insights.claim: Japan's Ministry for Economy, Trade and Industry has been restored as core planner and coordinator of an envisaged Y370 trillion (US$2.25 trillion) in public and private investment over 15 years across 17 designated strategic sectors.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A US$2.25tn state-coordinated capex pipeline is the single largest identifiable demand signal in Japan — sector inclusion on the strategic list is the key screening variable.
insights.quote: an envisaged Y370 trillion (US$2.25 trillion at today’s exchange rates) in public and private investment over the next 15 years in 17 sectors identified as strategic
insights.locator: Back from the days of the pre-1990s is the role of the Ministry

insights.claim: The 17 strategic sectors span artificial intelligence, quantum computing, semiconductors, fusion energy and defence alongside conventional areas such as 'the content industry' and 'information and communications'.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A concrete sector map for Japanese policy-supported capital flows; the mundane inclusions signal the list is a political consensus document rather than a sharp allocation.
insights.locator: The 17 sectors include sexy areas such as artificial intelligence

insights.claim: The breadth of the strategic sector list suggests the government widened it for fear of stigmatising any sector as non-strategic, diluting the plan's ability to pick winners.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Inclusion on the list is weak evidence of genuine policy prioritisation — differentiate by which sectors actually receive syndicated financing.
insights.quote: it can feel as if the government felt the need to be inclusive, for fear of stigmatising sectors as non-strategic
insights.locator: Looking at the list, it can feel as if the government

insights.claim: Economist Jesper Koll expects roughly 10 per cent of the Y370 trillion to come from on-balance-sheet national government debt, 60 per cent from private corporations, asset owners and investment managers, and 30 per cent from off-balance-sheet public-policy financing vehicles such as the Development Bank of Japan and Japan Investment Corporation.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Roughly Y222 trillion is assumed to come from private balance sheets — the plan's credibility hinges on corporate willingness to deploy, and the ex-FILP policy lenders are the vehicles to watch for issuance.
insights.quote: Of the Y370 trillion, I expect approximately 10% to come from on-balance-sheet national government debt, 60% from private corporations, asset owners and investment managers, and 30% coordinated and syndicated by off-balance-sheet
insights.locator: Jesper Koll, a veteran Japan-based economist

insights.claim: The purpose of a 15-year plan is less about the specific numbers than about providing a durability framework that convinces private investors policies will endure long enough to justify committing capital.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Policy-persistence signalling is the mechanism through which the plan crowds in private money; any political disruption to Takaichi undermines the whole structure.
insights.quote: the point of the long-term plan is to try to provide a framework that might convince investors that policies are going to endure
insights.locator: How much of that Y222 trillion or so of private investment

insights.claim: Japan's trend growth has been stuck just below one per cent a year for the past decade, and the real test of the industrial plan is whether it raises productivity growth enough to offset an ageing and shrinking population.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: The benchmark for judging Takanomics is productivity growth, not headline investment totals — a sub-1% baseline is the bar to beat.
insights.locator: It would be reasonable to have some doubts

insights.claim: The method behind Takaichi's plan draws on state-coordination techniques that worked in the very different circumstances of Japan's 1960s and 1970s high-growth heyday, when MITI ran industrial policy.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Catch-up-era planning tools applied to a frontier economy is the core scepticism case against Japanese industrial-policy equity narratives.
insights.quote: the method draws very much on techniques that proved successful in the rather different circumstances of the 1960s and 1970s
insights.locator: The ambition is impressive

themes.theme: Inflation, BoJ policy and the cost of capital

insights.claim: The Y370 trillion expansionary plan is bound to be inflationary in a Japan already running price inflation above both the Bank of Japan's two per cent target and nominal wage growth.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A structurally inflationary fiscal-industrial impulse argues against any return to sub-2% Japanese inflation and against long JGB duration.
insights.quote: this expansionary plan is bound to be inflationary, in a country which has already been grappling in recent years with price inflation that has been exceeding both the central bank’s two per cent target and nominal wage growth
insights.locator: Amid the uncertainties inevitably associated

insights.claim: For Takaichi's plan to work the Bank of Japan will have to raise interest rates enough to hold annual inflation at or below two per cent — directly contradicting her own leadership-campaign statements that rates should be kept low.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Expect BoJ tightening to continue despite dovish political rhetoric — a setup for yen strength and for repricing of the JGB curve.
insights.quote: it will be imperative that the Bank of Japan raise interest rates sufficiently to keep annual inflation to two per cent or below
insights.locator: So contrary to comments made by Takaichi during her campaign

insights.claim: The cost of capital will rise for both the Japanese government and the private sector, driven by the plan's high demand for funds and by the inflation compensation lenders will require.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Higher Japanese discount rates have global spillovers via repatriation of Japanese savings out of foreign bonds.
insights.locator: The other is that the cost of capital

insights.claim: Higher rates would improve capital allocation discipline in Japan after decades of low rates kept far too many inefficient and unproductive companies alive.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A rising cost of capital is a bullish structural catalyst for Japanese corporate restructuring, consolidation and equity returns on capital.
insights.quote: leaving far too many inefficient and unproductive companies alive
insights.locator: This could improve the allocation of capital

insights.claim: Rising rates will squeeze the Japanese government budget as the cost of servicing its huge debt stock increases, creating tension with the fiscal expansion the plan requires.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Debt-service arithmetic is the binding constraint on how far the BoJ can normalise — watch for fiscal dominance pressure on the central bank.
insights.locator: But it will also put more pressure on the government budget

themes.theme: Fiscal incoherence: tax cuts and the GPIF

insights.claim: Takaichi has insisted on cutting Japan's consumption tax on food from eight per cent to just one per cent, supposedly temporarily, while simultaneously announcing an ambitious fiscal-industrial plan.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A revenue-cutting measure layered onto a spending expansion weakens the fiscal anchor exactly as issuance needs rise — bearish for JGBs and the yen at the margin.
insights.quote: she has insisted on cutting the country’s consumption tax, which is currently 10 per cent for most items and eight per cent for food, to just one per cent for food, supposedly temporarily
insights.locator: That prospect has raised some quite serious doubts

insights.claim: The consumption tax cut is arriving just as Japanese household support is becoming unnecessary, because incomes have begun rising faster than inflation for the first time in several years.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Pro-cyclical stimulus into a genuine real-income recovery raises the odds of overheating and a faster BoJ path.
insights.quote: In recent months, incomes have begun to rise more rapidly than inflation for the first time in several years.
insights.locator: Takaichi may want to do this to reduce headline inflation

insights.claim: The OECD's recent economic survey found that domestic demand is now the main driver of Japanese growth for the first time since the country's financial crash began in 1990.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A 35-year regime change in Japan's growth composition — domestic cyclicals and services become the higher-beta expression of Japan rather than exporters.
insights.quote: domestic demand is now the main driver of growth, for the first time since the country’s financial crash began in 1990
insights.locator: As the OECD said in its recent economic survey of Japan

insights.claim: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama floated pressing the Government Pension Investment Fund, the world's largest retirement savings pool, to buy more Japanese government bonds, apparently anticipating that the Bank of Japan will reduce its purchases as it normalises policy.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: If the GPIF is redirected into JGBs it must sell or under-allocate to global equities and bonds — a material negative flow for non-Japanese risk assets.
insights.locator: A second sign of incoherence came from the Minister of Finance

insights.claim: Managing government borrowing costs by forcing the GPIF to earn lower returns for its beneficiaries would be a seriously retrograde step, evidence that Team Takaichi has not yet got its economic thinking straight.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Watch GPIF allocation reviews as the tell for whether Japan slides toward financial repression to fund the plan.
insights.quote: Despite the big fanfare around her new industrial policy, it feels as if Team Takaichi have not yet got their economic thinking straight.
insights.locator: Yet to try to manage the government’s borrowing costs

insights.claim: Japan has no viable alternative to sticking close to the United States because, unlike European NATO which could in principle cope with Russia alone, Japan on its own could not deter China.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Japan's negotiating leverage with Washington is structurally weaker than Europe's — expect Japan to absorb US demands rather than hedge away, capping any 'Japan decouples' thesis.
insights.quote: In principle European NATO could cope with Russia, but Japan on its own could not deter China.
insights.locator: Unlike the Europeans in NATO

insights.claim: The US-Japan Security Alliance looks more important to Japan now than at any time since its 1951 launch, precisely when America is behaving in more erratic and problematic ways than ever before.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Maximum dependence coinciding with maximum US unpredictability is the core tail risk for East Asian security pricing.
insights.quote: The US-Japan Security Alliance looks more important to Japan now than at any time since it was launched in 1951, just at a time when America itself is behaving in more erratic and problematic ways than ever before.
insights.locator: Unlike the Europeans in NATO

insights.claim: Japanese policy is moving in two directions at once: building capabilities that make Japan more valuable to the US as a deterrent against Chinese aggression over Taiwan, while simultaneously reducing long-term dependency on American technology and weapons supplies.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Both vectors mean sustained Japanese defence spending growth, with the second favouring domestic primes over US import programmes.

insights.so_what: Hyperscaler cloud wins in Japanese government are secure, but application-layer US vendors face a political ceiling — a specific negative read for Palantir's Japan expansion.

insights.claim: Japan is actively debating whether it is already too late to build its own foundational AI model in a public programme, or whether investing in a Japanese foundational model in parallel with American industry leaders is still prudent.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A live sovereign-AI funding decision in a G7 economy — a possible new source of national compute and model spending, or an explicit concession of the layer to US vendors.

insights.claim: Tokyo is now openly discussing formally revising the third of Japan's three non-nuclear principles established in 1967 by Eisaku Sato — the ban on permitting nuclear weapons to be brought into Japanese territory.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A formal change would be the most visible shift in Japanese nuclear posture in almost 60 years and a step-change signal in East Asian escalation risk.
insights.locator: The effort to be more valuable also contains a new nostalgic element

insights.claim: So-called Japanese 'nuclear sharing' would in practice mean only permitting America to move nuclear-armed vessels and aircraft through Japan — the only thing shared would be geography.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Headlines about Japanese nuclear sharing overstate the substance; the change is about legalising Cold War practice, not acquiring weapons.
insights.quote: The only thing that would be shared is geography.

insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Frames the proposed change as formalising an existing reality, lowering the probability of a dramatic regional reaction.

themes.theme: Building a Japanese external intelligence service

insights.claim: Japan passed a framework law in May placing a new intelligence set-up under a National Intelligence Council, aiming to build an external intelligence bureau modelled on Britain's MI6, though much of the structure remains vague.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A brand-new national intelligence build-out implies multi-year spending on recruitment, training, and secure technology procurement.
insights.locator: A framework law was passed in May

insights.claim: Since 1945 Japanese intelligence collection has been essentially domestic and run by the National Police Agency, overseen by a small Cabinet Office unit far weaker than America's Director of National Intelligence.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Japan is starting from near-zero external collection capability, meaning its independent read on China and North Korea will remain thin for years.
insights.locator: Since 1945, Japanese intelligence collection

insights.claim: The hardest constraint on Japan's new external bureau is human capital: it will probably need around 2,000 officers from almost a standing start, while the foreign ministry's existing intelligence-analysis section numbers about 100 people, none of whom run agents overseas.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A 20x staffing gap means the capability is a decade-plus project; do not expect Japanese autonomous intelligence to reduce US dependency this cycle.
insights.quote: the probably 2,000 officers such an external bureau will need if it is to be effective. The foreign ministry’s existing intelligence-analysis section numbers about 100 people, none of whom are running agents overseas
insights.locator: The most difficult task will be recruiting and training

insights.claim: The critical design test for Japan's new bureau is keeping it as separate from the National Police Agency as the CIA has been from the FBI since 1947, with placement under the Foreign Minister rather than the Ministry of Internal Affairs a promising sign.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: A concrete, observable indicator for judging whether Japan's intelligence reform is real: which ministry gets supervisory control.
insights.locator: The critical point may well be to avoid nostalgia

themes.theme: Imperial succession and Takaichi's political capital

insights.claim: Takaichi's February landslide gave the LDP a huge Lower House majority but she remains constrained by the party's lack of an Upper House majority, which cannot change until elections to that chamber in 2028.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Legislative capacity is asymmetric — big-bang reforms requiring both chambers face a hard 2028 gate, which caps the pace of Takanomics implementation.
insights.locator: That landslide victory did not make her impregnable

insights.claim: Takaichi's February electoral landslide was driven by her novelty as Japan's first non-dynastic female prime minister and by her robust stance in a row with China over remarks she made in the Diet about Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Confrontation with China is electorally rewarded in Japan, which raises the base rate of future Taiwan-related friction and China-Japan economic retaliation.
insights.locator: This was largely attributed to Takaichi’s novelty

insights.claim: Takaichi spent political capital pushing through an amendment to the 1947 Imperial Household Law allowing the imperial family to adopt males from 11 branch families excluded in 1947, rather than permitting female heirs.
insights.speaker: Bill Emmott
insights.so_what: Evidence that Takaichi will spend capital on conservative identity issues rather than economic reform — a discount factor on the reform premium in Japanese assets.

insights.so_what: A 30-plus point gap between public opinion and government policy is a measurable source of political fragility for the administration.
